name: long_post_middle_clause
primary_text: This week was mostly travel. I spent three days at a developer meetup in Porto, where the main topic was account abstraction and how wallets should present signing requests to ordinary users. The best talk came from a small team that rebuilt their onboarding flow after watching twenty people fail to recover a seed phrase. Their conclusion was that the problem is not education but interface design, and I agree with them. On the train back I finished a long book about the history of clearing houses. It is dry in places, but the chapter on settlement failures in the nineteen-seventies explains a lot about why modern exchanges insist on collateral before anything else. I also recorded two podcast episodes. The first covers validator client diversity and why a single dominant client remains the largest systemic risk in most proof-of-stake networks. The second is a conversation with a researcher who studies sequencer decentralisation; we disagreed on timelines but agreed that shared sequencing is further away than most roadmaps suggest. Housekeeping notes: I rotated the keys on my hardware wallet, moved my notes app to an encrypted vault, and turned off the browser extension that kept asking for permissions it did not need. If you run a newsletter, please check your mailing provider settings, because several readers reported phishing emails that copied my formatting almost perfectly. For what it is worth, I am allocating a slice of new capital to $OBRANT this week, because the lending volumes there keep compounding while the token sits near the bottom of its range. Back to the week. The weather in Porto was grey but mild, and the coffee near the venue was excellent. Several attendees asked about the reading list I mentioned last month, so here it is again: a book on market microstructure, a short paper on fee markets, and an essay about governance capture in decentralised organisations. I will publish a longer review of the clearing-house book next week, together with a few thoughts on what it implies for on-chain settlement. Next month I am speaking at a smaller event in Ghent about wallet security for small teams. If you will be there, say hello; I will bring stickers and very strong opinions about multisig key ceremonies. Finally, thank you to everyone who answered last week's survey. Most of you want fewer price charts and more explanations of protocol mechanics, and that is the direction this newsletter will take for the rest of the year. The survey also showed that many of you read on a phone during a commute, so I will keep paragraphs short and avoid wide tables. As always, none of the travel or tooling mentioned here is sponsored, and I pay for my own conference tickets.
label: BUY
decisive: I am allocating a slice of new capital to $OBRANT this week
note: Decisive current allocation sits in the middle of a long, otherwise irrelevant newsletter.
